body_html:
How to think about it

Coulomb's law: the force between two point charges is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them: F = kQ₁Q₂/r², with k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²·C⁻². Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.

An electric field is a region in which a charge experiences a force. Field lines point away from positive charges and towards negative charges. The field strength is E = F/q; for a point charge E = kQ/r².

Example

Charges are moved twice as far apart. New force?

1/2²

Answer: one quarter

Example

A 2 × 10⁻⁶ C charge feels 0,04 N. Field strength?

E = F/q

Answer: 2 × 10⁴ N·C⁻¹

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting to change µC to C.
  • Not squaring r.
  • Drawing field lines into a positive charge.

faq.q: Why do field lines never cross?
faq.a: At any point the field has only one direction.

faq.q: What is the field like between two parallel charged plates?
faq.a: Uniform: the lines are parallel and evenly spaced, from the positive plate to the negative plate.
